title: What I Told Oprah About Generational Differences in the Workplace -- and Beyond
author: Jean M. Twenge
summary: Jean Twenge recounts her appearance on Oprah's new online show, based on her book Generations, and summarizes the generational differences that interested people most. She notes there are now seven living generations, and that a Gen Z worker's explanation of the blank work stare shows lower expectations that work will be enjoyable. Using Monitoring the Future survey data since 1976, she says the clearest generational change in work attitudes is work-life balance, not wanting interesting jobs. She describes the slow life strategy: longer lives have slowed development, so kids are less independent and young adults marry later, which she says is not an economic effect. She links delayed dating partly to weaker social skills, notes Boomers' continued partying, and closes with impressions of Oprah as a skilled, kind interviewer.
points: Twenge says there are now seven living generations and that understanding real differences should help people understand one another.
Survey data since 1976 show Gen Z is less willing to work overtime and less likely to see work as central to life.
She explains the slow life strategy: with longer lifespans, adolescence and young adulthood are stretching out, and it is not driven by economics.
She ties part of Gen Z's delay in dating to a gap in social skills and less in-person socializing.
She closes with impressions of Oprah as a skilled interviewer who generously spent time with students.
quotes: There are now seven living generations: Silents, Boomers, Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z, Alphas, and Betas.

The co-existence of so many generations makes it even more important that we recognize what the real differences between generations are – not so we can point fingers, but so we can understand each other better.
A lot of it is hard to study, especially since any survey of workers done a single time can’t separate age from generation.

The biggest generational difference is instead in work-life balance: Especially post-pandemic, Gen Z is less likely to say they are willing to work overtime and less likely to say that they expect work to be a central part of their lives
Young people are not necessarily immature or “failing to launch” – they are just taking longer to grow to adulthood, just as their parents are taking longer to feel old.

With people living longer, the entire developmental trajectory has slowed down: Kids are less independent, teens are less likely to have a driver’s license or a job, young adults marry and have kids later, and middle-aged people look and feel younger than their parents or grandparents at the same age.
There’s also a gap in social skills, and meeting people to date is the ultimate test of social skills because much of the interaction is unspoken rather than said directly.
